```{python}
#| output: false
import os
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


def find_root() -> Path:
    here = Path.cwd().resolve()
    for cand in [here, *here.parents]:
        if (cand / "Makefile").exists() and (cand / "assignment.md").exists():
            return cand
    return here


ROOT = find_root()
DATA_DIR = Path(os.environ.get("DATA_DIR", ROOT / "data"))

SHORT = {
    "ITM-0426": "USB charger receptacle",
    "ITM-0311": "3-gang metal device box",
    "ITM-0612": "Copper lug, 2 AWG",
    "ITM-0237": "PVC conduit elbow",
    "ITM-0201": "EMT conduit, 1/2 in",
    "ITM-0621": "Butt splice, bag of 25",
    "ITM-0433": "Decora wall plate, white",
    "ITM-0434": "Decora wall plate, ivory",
    "ITM-1015": "Heat-shrink tubing",
    "ITM-0929": "Strut nut, 1/2 in",
    "ITM-0306": "Plastic old-work box",
    "ITM-0611": "Copper lug, 4 AWG",
}
MONTHS = ["January", "February", "March", "April", "May", "June",
          "July", "August", "September", "October", "November", "December"]
# Months that run high and are worth naming next to a buy recommendation,
# or that are the only timing note on an item with no cheap month.
AVOID = [
    ("ITM-0426", 6),
    ("ITM-0311", 5),
    ("ITM-0201", 3),
    ("ITM-0929", 4),
    ("ITM-0611", 11),
]

lines = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "gold" / "fct_company_a_purchase_line.csv", parse_dates=["order_date"])
lines = lines.loc[lines["status"] != "Cancelled"].copy()
lines["extended"] = lines["quantity_ordered"] * lines["unit_price_paid"]
n_orders = lines["po_number"].nunique()

items = lines.groupby("item_id", as_index=False).agg(
    n_orders=("po_number", "nunique"),
    n_months=("order_date", lambda s: s.dt.to_period("M").nunique()),
    first_order=("order_date", "min"),
    last_order=("order_date", "max"),
    total_spend=("extended", "sum"),
)
items["span_days"] = (items["last_order"] - items["first_order"]).dt.days
items["attachment"] = items["n_orders"] / n_orders
items["eligible"] = (items["n_months"] >= 8) & (items["span_days"] >= 365)
focus = items.loc[
    (items["attachment"] > items["attachment"].quantile(0.9))
    & items["eligible"]
    & (items["total_spend"] > items["total_spend"].median())
].copy()
focus_total_spend = float(focus["total_spend"].sum())

priced = lines.loc[lines["item_id"].isin(focus["item_id"])].dropna(subset=["unit_price_paid"]).copy()
priced["relative_price"] = (
    priced["unit_price_paid"] / priced.groupby("item_id")["unit_price_paid"].transform("median")
)
priced["year_month"] = priced["order_date"].dt.to_period("M").dt.to_timestamp()
item_month = priced.groupby(["item_id", "year_month"], as_index=False)["relative_price"].median()
month_index = pd.date_range(item_month["year_month"].min(), item_month["year_month"].max(), freq="MS")

frames = []
for item_id, group in item_month.groupby("item_id"):
    series = group.set_index("year_month")["relative_price"].reindex(month_index)
    series.index.name = "year_month"
    frame = series.rename("relative_price").reset_index()
    frame["item_id"] = item_id
    frames.append(frame)
by_item = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)


def straight_line(frame):
    mask = frame["relative_price"].notna().to_numpy()
    t = np.arange(len(frame), dtype=float)
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(t[mask], frame.loc[mask, "relative_price"].to_numpy(float), 1)
    return slope * t + intercept


pieces = []
for _, frame in by_item.groupby("item_id", sort=False):
    frame = frame.sort_values("year_month").copy()
    frame["detrended"] = frame["relative_price"] - straight_line(frame)
    pieces.append(frame)
detrended = pd.concat(pieces, ignore_index=True)
detrended["year"] = detrended["year_month"].dt.year
detrended["month"] = detrended["year_month"].dt.month

observed = (
    detrended.dropna(subset=["detrended"])
    .groupby(["item_id", "month", "year"], as_index=False)["detrended"]
    .mean()
)
month_gap = observed.groupby(["item_id", "month"], as_index=False).agg(
    n_years=("year", "nunique"),
    gap=("detrended", "mean"),
    years=("year", lambda s: ",".join(str(int(y)) for y in sorted(set(s)))),
    all_under=("detrended", lambda s: bool((s < 0).all())),
    all_over=("detrended", lambda s: bool((s > 0).all())),
)

median_price = priced.groupby("item_id")["unit_price_paid"].transform("median")
valued = priced.assign(
    month=priced["year_month"].dt.month,
    typical_extended=priced["quantity_ordered"] * median_price,
).merge(detrended[["item_id", "year_month", "detrended"]], on=["item_id", "year_month"])


def as_percent(value):
    points = abs(value) * 100
    if points < 1:
        return "under 1%"
    return f"{points:.0f}%"


def year_phrase(years):
    parts = years.split(",")
    if len(parts) == 1:
        return parts[0]
    if len(parts) == 2:
        return f"{parts[0]} and {parts[1]}"
    return ", ".join(parts[:-1]) + f", and {parts[-1]}"


def year_span(years):
    parts = years.split(",")
    if len(parts) == 1:
        return parts[0]
    return f"{parts[0]}-{parts[-1]}"


def cheap_savings(row):
    part = valued.loc[valued["item_id"] == row.item_id]
    outside = part["month"] != row.month
    return (
        part.loc[outside, "typical_extended"]
        * (part.loc[outside, "detrended"] - row.gap)
    ).sum()


def high_extra(item_id, month):
    part = valued.loc[(valued["item_id"] == item_id) & (valued["month"] == month)]
    return (part["typical_extended"] * part["detrended"]).sum()


cheap_rows = month_gap.loc[month_gap["all_under"]].copy()
cheap_rows["savings"] = cheap_rows.apply(cheap_savings, axis=1)
# More years first, then the deeper gap. One month per item.
chosen = (
    cheap_rows.sort_values(["item_id", "n_years", "gap"], ascending=[True, False, True])
    .groupby("item_id", as_index=False)
    .head(1)
    .set_index("item_id")
)
chosen["name"] = chosen.index.map(SHORT)
chosen["month_name"] = chosen["month"].map(lambda m: MONTHS[int(m) - 1])
chosen["gap_label"] = chosen["gap"].map(as_percent)
chosen["years_label"] = chosen["years"].map(year_phrase)

# About $50 over the whole history is where a repeated month is worth planning around.
recommend = chosen.loc[chosen["savings"] >= 50].sort_values("savings", ascending=False)
modest = chosen.loc[(chosen["savings"] >= 15) & (chosen["savings"] < 50)].sort_values("savings", ascending=False)
no_timing = chosen.loc[chosen["savings"] < 15].sort_values("savings", ascending=False)
# Sum the rounded dollars the table shows, so the headline matches the rows.
recommend_total = float(recommend["savings"].round(0).sum())
modest_total = float(modest["savings"].round(0).sum())
recommend_share = recommend_total / focus_total_spend

avoid_rows = []
for item_id, month in AVOID:
    gap_row = month_gap.loc[(month_gap["item_id"] == item_id) & (month_gap["month"] == month)].iloc[0]
    yearly = observed.loc[(observed["item_id"] == item_id) & (observed["month"] == month)]
    avoid_rows.append({
        "item_id": item_id,
        "name": SHORT[item_id],
        "month_name": MONTHS[month - 1],
        "gap": float(gap_row["gap"]),
        "gap_label": as_percent(gap_row["gap"]),
        "years": gap_row["years"],
        "years_label": year_phrase(gap_row["years"]),
        "extra": float(high_extra(item_id, month)),
        "by_year": {int(r.year): float(r.detrended) for r in yearly.itertuples(index=False)},
    })
avoid = pd.DataFrame(avoid_rows).set_index("item_id")

pooled = item_month.groupby("year_month")["relative_price"].median().reindex(month_index)
mask = pooled.notna().to_numpy()
t = np.arange(len(pooled), dtype=float)
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(t[mask], pooled.to_numpy(float)[mask], 1)
trend = pd.Series(slope * t + intercept, index=pooled.index)
rise_pct = trend.iloc[-1] / trend.iloc[0] - 1
rise_label = as_percent(rise_pct)
season = pd.DataFrame({
    "yoy": pooled.pct_change(12),
    "detrended": pooled - trend,
})
season["year"] = season.index.year
season["month"] = season.index.month

frequent_share = float(items["attachment"].quantile(0.9))
screen = {
    "n_orders": int(n_orders),
    "n_items": int(len(items)),
    "n_eligible": int(items["eligible"].sum()),
    "frequent_share": frequent_share,
    "frequent_orders": frequent_share * n_orders,
    "spend_cutoff": float(items["total_spend"].median()),
    "n_focus": int(len(focus)),
    "min_focus_spend": float(focus["total_spend"].min()),
    "max_attachment": float(focus["attachment"].max()),
    "start": lines["order_date"].min().strftime("%B %Y"),
    "end": lines["order_date"].max().strftime("%B %Y"),
}


def money(item_id, frame=chosen):
    return f"${frame.loc[item_id, 'savings']:,.0f}"


def dollars(amount):
    return f"${amount:,.0f}"
```

## Executive Summary & Actionable Recommendations

There is no calendar month in which the items you buy most often are cheaper as a group. Seasonality, where it exists, belongs to the individual item, not to the catalog. Set purchase timing item by item, and only for the items below. For everything else, buy when the job requires the material. Chasing a calendar month on an item with no proven pattern will not save money and may cost time.

Four directives, based on `{python} f"{screen['n_orders']:,}"` orders across `{python} screen["n_items"]` items, `{python} screen["start"]` through `{python} screen["end"]`:

- **Shift five items to the months below, when the schedule allows it.** These are the only items with a repeated, same-direction price gap in every year on record. Moving the remaining purchases of these five items into their low month would have saved `{python} dollars(recommend_total)` on this history.
- **Do not extend this logic to similar items.** Matching descriptions do not share a cheap month. The two Decora wall plates, the two copper lugs, and the metal and plastic device boxes each point in different directions or show no pattern at all.
- **Treat the two-year patterns as provisional, not settled.** Three of the five recommendations below rest on two years of data, not three. Confirm November and September behave the same way once the 2026 data for those months exists before locking them into a standing purchasing calendar.
- **Do not set a minimum order size to chase a volume discount.** Larger orders have sometimes carried a lower price in this data, but the pattern is not consistent as quantity increases: price drops, then rises, then drops again. It is not a reliable rule and should not drive order consolidation on its own.

```{python}
#| output: asis

header = (
    "| Item | Buy in | Below trend | Years of evidence | Saving |\n"
    "|---|---|---:|---|---:|"
)
rows = []
for item_id, row in recommend.iterrows():
    rows.append(
        f"| {row['name']} ({item_id}) | {row['month_name']} | {row['gap_label']} "
        f"| {year_span(row['years'])} | {money(item_id)} |"
    )
print("\n".join([header, *rows]))
```

The saving is the gap between the price paid in other months and the low month, valued at the item's usual unit price. Units already purchased in the named month are excluded, so this is money left on the table, not a rebuild of full spend.

## Financial & Operational Impact

Retiming these five items would have saved `{python} dollars(recommend_total)` against `{python} dollars(round(focus_total_spend))` in spend on the twelve items reviewed, about `{python} f"{recommend_share:.1%}"` of that spend. Three further items show the same repeated pattern but not enough dollars to justify changing a process: the butt splice (August), the white wall plate (February), and the ivory wall plate (June), worth `{python} dollars(modest_total)` together. The remaining four reviewed items showed no month worth planning around; moving their purchases to the closest thing to a low month would have cost money, not saved it.

This saving only converts to cash if two conditions hold: the job using the item can move by one or two months, or the material can be held without extra carrying cost that erases the saving, and the purchasing team actually tracks the five months rather than treating this as a one-time note. A job that cannot wait for July to buy the metal box should still buy the metal box when it is needed.

A second, smaller cost is avoidable the same way: five items plus EMT conduit and the strut nut run measurably above trend in specific months (table below). Steering discretionary orders away from those months, where the schedule permits, avoids a premium without any new tracking beyond the buy list already in place.

## Supporting Data

Two charts and two tables from the underlying analysis carry the argument and are kept below. Everything else in the notebook, the catalog-wide histograms used to set the frequency and spend thresholds, the manufacturer and vendor breakdowns, the twelve-panel per-item and per-month grids, and the quantity and day-of-week charts, is an internal diagnostic and is dropped from this brief. The quantity chart is dropped as a headline visual specifically because its pattern is not monotonic and should not be read as a pricing rule; it is addressed as a caveat, not evidence, in Risk & Limitations.

- **Savings-by-item chart** (below). Ranks all twelve reviewed items by dollars at stake, so it is clear at a glance which five are worth a process change.
- **Seasonal evidence chart** (below). Shows the three years of data do not move together, which is the direct answer to whether a portfolio-wide low season exists.
- **Recommendation and caution tables** (above and below). Compact, dollar-denominated, and map directly to an action.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 6.4

fig.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
handles, labels = axes[1].get_legend_handles_labels()
fig.legend(handles, labels, loc="upper center", ncol=3, frameon=False, fontsize=8, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.1))
```

The price level itself has risen about `{python} rise_label` from the start of 2024 to `{python} screen["end"]`. A January that looks inexpensive in raw dollars is mostly that rise, not a seasonal discount. Every number in this brief is measured after removing it.

```{python}
#| output: asis

header = (

    "|---|---|---:|---|---:|"
)
```

June for the USB charger is the only row above with real money on it, `{python} dollars(avoid.loc["ITM-0426", "extra"])`, already folded into the `{python} money("ITM-0426")` November recommendation, not counted twice. ## Risk & Limitations

- **The strongest single number rests on the thinnest evidence.** The USB charger's `{python} money("ITM-0426")` November saving is the largest in the table, but it comes from only two Novembers (2024 and 2025), and those two years do not agree closely: about 2% under trend in 2024, about 6% under in 2025. The PVC conduit elbow's September figure and the copper lug's November figure are also two-year patterns. Treat these three as a working hypothesis to confirm in 2026, not a locked rule.
- **This is a description of orders already placed, not a forecast.** November 2026 and the rest of the fourth quarter have not happened. Nothing here predicts what a vendor will charge next quarter; it summarizes what Company A paid in the past.
- **Vendor discounts and negotiation are invisible in this data.** The analysis compares prices Company A actually paid to Company A's own history. It cannot tell whether a low month reflects the vendor's list price moving or a one-off concession Company A negotiated that will not repeat. A vendor could offer a better deal in any month for reasons this history will not show.
- **Macro and commodity moves are not separated out.** Copper, freight, and broader market pricing can shift a unit price for reasons that have nothing to do with the calendar. A monthly pattern that lines up with a commodity cycle could look like seasonality here and be something else entirely.
- **Holding and schedule costs are not in the model.** A low month only pays off if the job can move by a month or two, or if the material can sit in inventory without added carrying cost, storage risk, or damage. Neither is quantified here; both belong to the procurement and project teams' judgment.
- **The quantity pattern is noisy and should not be treated as a fact.** Larger orders have sometimes shown a lower unit price at the higher end of order sizes seen in this data, but the relationship does not move in one direction: price drops, rises again, and drops again as order size increases further. Day of week shows no effect. Neither finding is verified against vendor pricing terms and neither should be used to set an order-size policy today.
- **Similar items are not a guide to each other.** The white and ivory Decora wall plates, the two copper lug gauges, and the metal and plastic device boxes are close substitutes in the catalog and still do not share a cheap month, and in the case of the two lugs, point in opposite directions in the same month. Do not extend a finding on one item to a similar one without checking it separately.

**Scope of this review.** Cancelled orders are excluded. An item entered the review only if it was frequent (top 10% of orders by attachment, at least `{python} f"{screen['frequent_share']:.1%}"` of orders), had enough history to compare a season (purchased in at least 8 distinct months across at least a year), and carried enough spend to be worth a better price (above the catalog's median item spend). `{python} screen["n_focus"]` items cleared all three tests; the five recommendations and three marginal cases above are drawn from that set of twelve.
